Gave GLM-5.2 and Opus 4.8 the same one-shot prompt for a playable Backrooms game, here's how they did:

GLM-5.2 just beat Claude Opus 4.8 on a one-shot game build.

Same prompt. No edits. No follow-ups.

Task: build a playable Backrooms horror game
in one HTML file.

GLM-5.2: all mechanics. Run. Pause. Flashlight.
Complete on the first try. Faster. Way cheaper.

Opus 4.8: flashlight worked.
Run and pause were missing on the first pass.

Both produced something playable — which is still
wild to say about a one-shot prompt.

But GLM-5.2 was more complete.

The Chinese open-weight tier is not catching up
to frontier models anymore.

In some specific workloads, it's ahead.

Full prompt in the comments if you want to run
your own bake-off. One OpenAI-compatible key runs both.

What's your go-to for one-shot "build me a whole thing"?

GLM-5.2 cooking up a clean, modern landing page in one shot... and it looks basically identical to what Opus 4.8 spit out. Open weights, 1M context, and like 6-8x cheaper.

I'm definitely firing this one up right after my Claude sub renews. Open-source front-end game is getting scary good. 😊

data.text:
How I Built Safar With Figma Make, Figma Weavy, MCP, Supabase, Firecrawl, AWS Rekognition, Stripe, Canva, and GitHub

This document explains how I built Safar for the Figma hackathon.

It is written as a practical build story, not a technical code document. The goal is to show how I used Figma Make, Figma Weavy, clear product instructions, focused prompting, MCP-connected tools, Supabase, Firecrawl, AWS Rekognition, Stripe, Canva, GitHub, and continuous testing to move from idea to working product flow quickly.

I Started With a Clear Product Definition

Before building screens or connecting backend tools, I first defined what Safar needed to be.

Safar is a tourist e-visa eligibility checker and assisted application platform. It helps travelers check whether they can apply, understand which documents they need, upload those documents, pay transparently, and track application status in one place.

The early product rules kept the whole build focused:

Eligibility checking should work without login.
One account should manage multiple family members.
Every application should be reviewed by a real human before submission.
Fees should always be transparent: government fee, Safar service fee, and total.
Applicant, admin, and partner flows should stay separate.
Status should always use icon, color, and text, not color alone.
The product should feel calm, trustworthy, and simple because visa applications are high-stakes.

These rules became the foundation for the full app.

I Created the Guidelines First

The first major step was creating a guidelines.md document inside Figma Make.

I used it as the product and design rulebook for Safar. It included:

Product purpose
Brand colors
Typography
Layout rules
Card, button, input, progress bar, and status badge behavior
Mobile-first design rules
Navigation rules
Fee display rules
Applicant, admin, and partner role rules
Things that should never be changed

This helped Figma Make keep the design consistent across the app instead of creating random layouts for every screen.

The design direction was:

Deep green for trust
Warm gold as an accent
Warm off-white background
Inter font
Mobile-first layout around a 390px baseline
Clear cards, simple inputs, visible progress, and readable status badges

I did not treat the guidelines as a one-time file. I improved them through conversation first, then started asking Figma Make to build screens.

I Saved the Core Documents Before Building

Before starting the actual design and build, I saved the important planning documents in the project workspace so I could keep referring back to them.

These documents included:

Product guidelines
First Figma Make prompt
Build process notes
Security notes
Testing notes
Landing page copy
Video script
Data pipeline plan
Visual and video scene workflow notes

This helped me avoid losing context and made the workflow more structured. Whenever I needed to improve a screen or flow, I could refer back to the same product rules instead of explaining everything again from scratch.

I Used Supabase as the Backend Foundation

After the product flow and design direction were clear, I used Supabase as the backend foundation.

Supabase handled the core backend needs:

User authentication
Session restoration
Applicant, admin, and partner roles
Application records
Family member records
Document checklist storage
Private document file storage
Application status updates
Edge Functions for backend actions

The product needed separate flows for applicants, admins, and partners, so role-based access was important from the beginning.

Applicants could start or resume applications, upload documents, pay fees, track status, and view approved visa documents.

Admins could review applications, check uploaded documents, request changes, approve documents, upload visa outcomes, and update application status.

Partners had a limited dashboard where they could only see assigned applications and perform limited actions.

I Used Figma Make to Generate Supabase Table Prompts

One part that helped me move quickly was using Figma Make to prepare the Supabase database structure.

Instead of manually planning every table from scratch, I asked Figma Make to generate ready-to-use Supabase SQL prompts for the database tables.

Figma Make helped prepare the table structure for:

User profiles
Applications
Application members
Documents
Country requirements
Requirement reviews
Scrape logs
Roles and statuses

I then copied the generated SQL into Supabase and ran it there. The tables were created quickly, and I did not face schema bugs during that step.

This saved setup time and helped me move faster from idea to working product flow.

I Connected Supabase With MCP to Speed Up Backend Work

After the tables were ready, I connected Supabase through MCP-supported tooling so the AI-assisted workflow could help with backend implementation faster.

This made it easier to connect the frontend flow with backend actions.

Using Supabase MCP and connected tooling helped move faster on:

Authentication
Role-based routing
Application creation
Document upload flow
Payment flow connection
Application status updates
Edge Function setup
Admin and partner dashboard behavior

This was useful because I did not have to manually translate every product requirement into backend structure from scratch.

I Used Edge Functions for Server-Side Workflows

For backend workflows that should not run directly in the frontend, I used Supabase Edge Functions.

These supported important product actions such as:

Creating applications
Uploading documents
Starting payment checkout
Handling Stripe payment confirmation
Updating application status
Supporting admin actions
Connecting Firecrawl live data lookup

This helped keep sensitive work on the server side and kept the frontend cleaner.

I Built the Figma Make Prototype Section by Section

After the guidelines were ready, I started building the screens in Figma Make.

The homepage was built around a calm, trust-focused message. It included:

A clear hero section
Primary call-to-action
Animated nationality text concept
Destination country cards
Live fee display
Coming soon country chips
How-it-works section
Footer and bottom navigation

Then I moved into the eligibility flow:

Select nationality
Select destination
Select visa duration or travel details
Add traveler details
View eligibility result
Start application after login or sign-up

The key rule was that eligibility checking should not require login. That was repeated often because it was one of the most important product decisions.

I Created Consistent Visuals and Video Scenes With Figma Weavy

Alongside the product screens, I created consistent visual assets and video scenes for Safar. This helped make the hackathon submission feel more complete and visually connected.

I used Figma Weavy as part of the visual creation workflow. Inside that workflow, I used Google Imagen4 to create consistent and accurate images that matched the Safar product story and brand direction.

Before generating the visuals, I first created the character and scene direction in Claude. I used Claude to prepare:

Positive prompts for the characters
Negative prompts to avoid inconsistent or unwanted results
Character consistency notes
Scene-by-scene visual direction
Clear image style instructions

After that, I generated the character references and downloaded the strongest outputs. I then imported those references into Figma Weavy.

To keep the scenes consistent, I used Cedence Reference 2.0 through the reference loader. I attached the reference images with the prompts so the new scenes could follow the same character identity, style, and visual direction.

The process was:

Create character direction in Claude.
Write positive and negative prompts for consistency.
Generate strong reference images with Google Imagen4 inside Figma Weavy.
Download the best character references.
Import the references back into Figma Weavy.
Attach the references to scene prompts using Cedence Reference 2.0.
Convert the reference images into different scenes.
Combine the scenes in Canva.
Export the final visuals or video assets.
Upload the final assets to the website or submission materials.

This helped me avoid random visuals. Instead of generating every image from scratch, I reused reference-based prompting so the characters, mood, and visual story stayed consistent across scenes.

I Integrated Firecrawl for Live Visa Requirement Data

Firecrawl was added to support live visa requirement and fee lookup.

The goal was to avoid relying only on static visa information.

The flow was:

The frontend asks for eligibility or fee information.
The Supabase Edge Function checks cached data first.
If the data is missing or outdated, Firecrawl searches or scrapes official visa information sources.
The result is normalized into the format the app needs.
The data is cached for around 48 hours.
The UI can show whether the result came from live lookup or fallback data.

I also included an admin-facing live data toggle so Firecrawl usage could be paused or resumed to manage credits.

I Used AWS Rekognition for Identity Liveness Verification

To add a layer of identity confidence before the human review step, I integrated AWS Rekognition for face liveness detection.

The liveness check was triggered at the point of application submission to verify that a real person was submitting the application.

The flow was:

The applicant is prompted to complete a face liveness session before submission.
The frontend uses the AWS Amplify FaceLivenessDetector component to capture the session.
The session result is sent to a Supabase Edge Function for server-side verification.
AWS Rekognition returns a confidence score confirming whether the session was live.
If liveness is confirmed above the required threshold, the application moves forward.
If the check fails or the confidence is too low, the applicant is asked to retry.

This helped protect the platform from fraudulent or bot-submitted applications without adding significant friction to the genuine applicant experience.

I Used Stripe Sandbox for Payments

Stripe sandbox was used to build and test the payment flow safely before production.

The payment flow was designed around transparency:

User reviews the government fee.
User reviews the Safar service fee.
User sees the total.
User accepts the no-refund policy.
User is redirected to Stripe Checkout.
Stripe confirms payment.
The application status updates after successful payment.

Stripe Checkout was used instead of collecting card details directly in the app.

The Stripe webhook was connected through the backend so the application could still be marked as paid and submitted even if the browser redirect failed.

I Used GitHub as Part of the Build Environment

GitHub was connected as part of the broader build and deployment environment.

It helped keep the project organized and ready for versioning, deployment, and future collaboration.

The main development process was driven through Figma Make, Supabase, MCP tooling, and connected services, while GitHub supported the overall project workflow.

I Built the Applicant Dashboard Around the Real User Flow

The applicant dashboard was built around what users actually need after checking eligibility.

The dashboard supported:

Starting a new application
Resuming a draft application
Uploading required documents
Paying application fees
Tracking application status
Viewing payment status
Viewing approved visa documents when available

The application flow inside the dashboard was simplified into:

Trip setup
Documents
Payment
Application tracking

This kept the user journey easy to understand.

I Built the Document Flow Around Occupation-Based Requirements

The document checklist was generated based on the applicant's profile and occupation.

Base required documents included:

Passport
CNIC or national ID
Passport-size photograph
Bank statement
Return flight ticket
Hotel or accommodation proof

Occupation-specific documents included:

Employment letter for job holders
Salary slips for job holders
Business proof for business owners
Enrollment letter for students
NOC for government employees

This made the product more useful than a generic checklist because different applicants need different documents.

I Improved the Upload Flow After Testing

During testing, some document upload states needed improvement.

Instead of rebuilding the whole flow, I focused on the specific upload problem.

The improvements included:

Making sure loading states always clear after upload success or failure
Adding upload timeout behavior
Compressing large camera images before upload
Showing faster previews
Marking documents as uploaded immediately after success
Moving users to the next pending document faster

This made the document flow feel smoother and more reliable.

I Created Separate Admin and Partner Dashboards

The admin and partner dashboards were kept separate from the applicant flow.

Admin dashboard capabilities included:

View application queue
Review uploaded documents
Request document changes
Upload approved visa documents
Approve or update application status

Partner dashboard restrictions included:

Partners only see assigned applications.
Partners cannot access full admin review tools.
Partners cannot manage other partners.
Partners cannot access monitoring sections.
Partners can update status, request documents, and add notes.

This helped keep access clear and safer.

I Tested Before Making Changes

One important practice I followed was testing or checking the current state before making changes.

Before asking Figma Make or the AI assistant to update something, I first looked at what was already working and what was not.

For example, before changing a flow or screen, I checked:

What the user currently sees
Which step is working
Which part feels confusing
Whether the issue is visual, product-related, or technical
Whether the change could break another screen or flow

This helped avoid unnecessary changes. Instead of rebuilding a whole page, I could fix the exact problem.

The same approach was used after changes as well. I tested the main flows again to confirm the update actually worked.

I Did Not Try to Do Too Much in One Prompt

One of the biggest lessons was to avoid overloading a single prompt.

Instead of asking Figma Make to create too many flows, screens, states, and backend assumptions in one message, I broke the work into smaller parts.

The better approach was:

Build one screen or section at a time.
Give a clear problem statement.
Mention the exact user goal.
Mention what should be changed.
Mention what should not be changed.
Review the output before moving to the next part.

This made the AI output cleaner and easier to control.

For example, instead of asking for the whole application flow at once, I worked through the product in focused parts:

Homepage
Eligibility checker
Eligibility result
Sign-up flow
Applicant dashboard
Document checklist
Document upload
Payment summary
Admin dashboard
Partner dashboard

This kept the design and logic more stable.

I Used Clear Problem Statements

Whenever something needed improvement, I tried to explain the problem clearly instead of saying only “make it better.”

A useful prompt included:

What is wrong right now
Why it matters for the user
What outcome I want
Which part should stay the same

For example, if the fee section was too crowded, the prompt needed to explain that users may miss the total amount and that the hierarchy should be improved while keeping the three-line fee breakdown.

This made the AI behave more like a product teammate instead of randomly redesigning things.

I Used User Stories and Acceptance Criteria

For important flows, I used a user-story style.

Example:

As an applicant, I want to check my visa eligibility without creating an account, so I can understand my options before sharing personal details.

Acceptance criteria:

The user can start from the homepage.
The user can select passport, destination, and occupation.
The user can see the result without login.
The result shows required documents, fees, and processing time.
Login is only required when starting the application.

This helped the AI understand the product logic, not only the visual layout.

I Used Component Selection for Targeted Edits

When a screen needed improvement, I did not always rewrite the full prompt.

For small fixes, I edited directly.

For more complex fixes, I selected the exact component or section inside Figma Make and asked AI to improve only that part.

Examples:

Select a card and ask it to improve readability.
Select the fee section and ask it to improve hierarchy.
Select a form and ask it to make labels clearer.
Select a status badge and ask it to use icon, color, and text.

This reduced the chance of the AI changing unrelated parts of the design.

I Cleared the Chat After Every Few Prompts

Another practice that worked well was clearing the chat after every two or three prompts.

This helped keep the context clean and reduced prompt drift.

My workflow was:

Ask for a focused update.
Review the output.
Edit small things manually.
Ask for one targeted improvement if needed.
Clear the chat after the section felt stable.
Continue with the next screen or flow.

This made the AI follow the latest design patterns without carrying too much old context.

I Tested the Main Flows Before Finalizing

Testing was part of the process, not only something at the end.

The key flows I checked included:

Eligibility checker without login
Account creation
Single applicant application flow
Family application flow
Document upload
Document re-upload after rejection
Admin application review
Requirement change review
Liveness check behavior
Telegram update flow
Mobile browser experience
Stripe sandbox payment flow

Before changing important parts, I checked what was already working. After changing them, I tested again to make sure the fix did not break the journey.

What Made This Workflow Work

The process worked because I did not treat AI as a one-shot builder.

I treated it like a product team assistant.

The most useful practices were:

Start with clear product rules.
Create guidelines before asking for screens.
Test before changing things.
Do not put too much into one prompt.
Build one screen or section at a time.
Use clear problem statements.
Use user stories and acceptance criteria.
Select components for focused edits.
Edit small things manually.
Clear chat context after every few prompts.
Use Figma Weavy, Google Imagen4, reference images, and Canva for consistent visual assets.
Use MCP and connected tools for faster backend setup.
Use Supabase SQL prompts to quickly create the backend structure.
Use Firecrawl for live data instead of relying only on static content.
Use Stripe sandbox before production payments.
Keep testing the actual user flow.

Reusable Process for Future Builds

This same process can be reused for other products:

Define the product in one clear paragraph.

Lock the most important product rules.

Create a guidelines file before designing screens.

Save supporting documents in the workspace.

Build one screen or section at a time.

Use focused prompts with clear outcomes.

Test the current state before making changes.

Select components for targeted improvements.

Clear the chat after every few prompts.

Use AI to generate backend structure and setup prompts.

Copy reviewed setup prompts into tools like Supabase where needed.

Connect MCP tools to speed up implementation.

Use external services only where they solve a real product problem.

Test the end-to-end user journey before final submission.

Companion Documentation I Created for Reuse
Alongside this Safar-specific hackathon process, I also created a shorter reusable AI build playbook that can be shared with other founders, builders, or teams.

The companion document removes Safar-specific implementation details and turns the workflow into a repeatable process for other use cases, such as:

SaaS products
Landing pages
Mobile app prototypes
Admin dashboards
Document upload and OCR flows
Internal tools
Marketplace products
Hackathon builds

The purpose of the companion document is to show the process behind the build, not the private code or technical setup.

It explains how to start with a guidelines file, build in small prompts, test before changing, use component-level edits, and connect tools like Supabase MCP, GitHub, Firecrawl, Stripe, and backend functions only when the product flow needs them.

Support file you can reuse for any other project with best practices: https://t.co/v8WCpsq9V1

Final Summary

I built Safar by combining product thinking, Figma Make, focused prompting, Supabase, MCP-connected tools, Firecrawl, AWS Rekognition, Stripe sandbox, GitHub, Canva, Figma Weavy, and continuous testing.

The most important part was not asking AI to do everything at once.

I created clear guidelines first, built section by section, tested before changing, used focused prompts, and connected the right backend tools only when the product flow needed them.

This process helped me move quickly while still keeping the product structured, understandable, and ready to explain as part of the Figma hackathon submission.

By the end of 2026 that number will hit 90%.

Most operators hear this stat and panic. 

They think the platform is saturated. 

They think the opportunity is gone. 

They quit before they even start.

Same templated title structures. 

Same recycled thumbnail formats.

The platform will keep paying out for high-effort AI content because real viewers still watch it and advertisers still pay for it.

The 90% flood is coming. 

Most operators will get washed away in it. 

The operators who learn to differentiate inside the flood will own the next decade of YouTube.

Stop fearing the flood. Start building inside it.

The opportunity is bigger than it has ever been.

US gov blocks Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5.  
@Zai_org drops GLM 5.2 with the "future of AI is open and belongs to the people" line.  

I watched the full review. Here's the unfiltered breakdown.

**Access and limits**  
• Gated behind paid GLM coding plans only. No regular chat. No API.  
• Price doubled to $65/month. Rate limits still brutal - multi-agent work gets throttled fast.

**Vibe-coding tests (Fable 5 project recreations)**  
• Horror game: keys collected, but monster chase and house exit never fired. Visually weaker.  
• Stealth-action: screen stayed almost pitch black. Lighting system failed completely.  
• Minecraft clone: launched fine. Character couldn't move.  
• Remotion video: mid output. Zero creativity, sloppy UI details.

**Bench results flipped the script**  
• Speed: almost 3x previous version - 296 tokens/sec.  
• Reasoning: #1 place. Beat Fable 5 on complex code logic.  
• BS-benchmark: perfect 100% for the first time. Handles nonsense inputs without hallucinating.  
• Hallucinations: 6th. Refactoring: 4th. Respectable numbers.

**Verdict**  
It misses the obsessive detail and one-shot reliability of real frontier models like Opus 4.8. You prompt, clarify, prompt again.  

Speed, logic, and price still make it a killer auxiliary agent in setups like Hermes - fast debugging, data analysis, simple tasks.  

Frontier models deliver one clean shot.  
GLM 5.2 delivers fast, honest iterations at scale.

I gave all three the same five build tasks. Same prompts, one shot each.

GLM 5.2 won the runner game by a mile. Opus looked slow and flat.
